opening.headline: We explore the reason why requests converge on a single point despite running multiple model servers, and how the inference gateway addresses this issue.
body: We increased the number of LLM model server pods to four, yet only one pod's queue grew longer while the other GPUs remained idle. Imagine users experiencing slow responses and timeouts, while the dashboard shows a sufficient number of pods. This imbalance arises because the request distribution mechanism fails to account for the actual load within the server.

In this lesson, we examine the Gateway API Inference Extension for self-hosted generative models in Kubernetes. We will sequentially review what components make up an inference gateway, what roles the InferencePool—responsible for routing targets—and the InferenceObjective—responsible for setting processing priority—each play, and how the llm-d router relates to this configuration. Finally, we will illustrate with a case study why routing considerations based on request length and queue state are necessary.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can describe the roles of InferencePool and the inference gateway.
General load balancing and inference routing can be distinguished.

screens.title: The model server consists of multiple instances, but requests are consolidated into a single point.
screens.lead: First, review common scenarios you encounter during operation. While examining the diagram to see how queue lengths differ across pods, consider what might be causing the issue.

visual.alt: A diagram showing thick request arrows converging on only one of four model server pods.
labels: Queue growing, KV cache almost full

paragraphs: A team launched four vLLM model server pods. The server count was increased sufficiently, but over time, only one pod's queue continued to grow longer, while the GPUs in the other three pods remained idle.

From the user's perspective, responses become slower, and some requests are terminated due to timeout. Adding more pods often leads to the same issue recurring. The problem lies not in the number of servers, but in how requests are distributed.

A general load balancer knows how many pods are behind it, but it does not know what is happening inside each pod. Since it does not receive signals indicating queue length or KV cache utilization, it may appear evenly distributed externally, but the actual load is not balanced.
This course covers how the biased inference gateway reduces bias.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: If we divide the request count equally, will the load also be equally distributed? Will the cost incurred by the server be the same for a short question and a lengthy document summary?

screens.outro: First, let's recall the role of the load balancer you are already familiar with.

screens.title: What is the load balancer in front of the model server?
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thought process unfolds. Please first think through the answer mentally before clicking it in.

items.prompt: Can you explain what the load balancer does in front of the model server? On what basis are requests routed to which pod?
items.answer: General load balancers or proxies select backend servers based on criteria such as request path, headers, or order (e.g., round-robin). NGINX is a typical example of a reverse proxy. These criteria have no relation to how busy the server currently is.

items.prompt: Are general web requests and LLM requests processed at the same cost?
items.answer: Yes. General web requests typically complete within a similar short duration, but LLM requests can vary significantly in the amount of time they occupy a GPU, depending on input length and the length of generated output. Even for the same request, some may involve short questions, while others involve lengthy document summaries.

items.prompt: Does a load balancer know about the queue or cache status of pods?
items.answer: A general load balancer typically does not know. As a result, when requests are processed sequentially, the pod that receives a long request ends up delaying all subsequent short requests. This course begins with the recognition that an additional step is required to assess and select based on server status.

screens.outro: Let's examine the component that reads signals the load balancer cannot see.

screens.title: Inference Gateway Composition: Gateway and Endpoint Picker
screens.lead: Let's walk step by step along the path from the client to the model server. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

visual.alt: The flow where a client's request goes through the gateway and Endpoint Picker to a pod in the model server pool.

steps.title: Extends the existing gateway
steps.body: The Inference Gateway does not start from scratch by building a new proxy. Instead, it combines Endpoint Picker (EPP) with Envoy's ext-proc (External Processing) protocol and Gateway API support, extending existing gateways such as Envoy Gateway, kgateway, and GKE Gateway.

steps.title: The request arrives at the gateway
steps.body: Client requests typically arrive at the gateway as usual. This project aims to expose a self-hosted model to other workloads in a manner similar to an OpenAI-compatible chat completion endpoint. Instead of merely inspecting the request path, the gateway can inspect the model name and route accordingly, and it also handles models fine-tuned with LoRA in the same way.

steps.title: EPP intercepts the request and receives a query.
steps.body: The gateway invokes EPP via ext-proc. EPP is a component that acts as a router, determining the most appropriate endpoint for a given request based on the metrics and functional information provided by the model server. The objective is to select the option with the lowest cost or the best performance.

steps.title: EPP reads the server status signal.
steps.body: The signals that EPP references are KV cache utilization, number of pending requests, active LoRA adapters, and prefix cache status. These are entirely different types of information from what a general load balancer sees in terms of paths or order. To expose these signals, the model server must adhere to the model server protocol defined by the project.

steps.title: Is delivered to the selected pod
steps.body: When EPP selects one replica, the gateway forwards the request to that pod. A pod with a short queue and available cache is chosen, thus dispersing requests that previously would have been concentrated on a single pod. The goal is to reduce tail latency and improve GPU utilization.

screens.outro: The bundle of candidates selected by EPP is the InferencePool. Let's examine the settings.

screens.title: InferencePool: A group of pods serving the same model
screens.lead: Select one phrase from the following InferencePool manifest and verify the role of each field.

visual.alt: The figure shows the three fields of InferencePool corresponding to pod group, port, and EPP respectively.

data.text:
apiVersion: inference.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: InferencePool
metadata:
  name: vllm-qwen3-32b
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: vllm-qwen3-32b
  targetPorts:
    - number: 8000
  endpointPickerRef:
    name: vllm-qwen3-32b-epp
    port:
      number: 9002
    failureMode: FailOpen

marks.note: This condition selects pods by label. Only pods within the same namespace can be selected, and the label must match exactly with the label attached to the model server pod. If it does not match, no pod will be selected in the pool.
The port number sent to the pod by the gateway. Here, it is forwarded to port 8000 of the selected pod. Each port is treated as a separate endpoint by the EPP.
This is a reference to the EPP service responsible for endpoint selection of the pool. Requests coming to this pool are routed based on a query to port 9002 of vllm-qwen3-32b-epp.

This describes the behavior when EPP fails to select or fails to respond to an endpoint. If FailOpen is set, the gateway forwards the request to an endpoint it selects on its own. Conversely, if FailClose is set, the gateway discards the request.

screens.outro: If InferencePool is determined to be sent somewhere, the decision of what to process first is made by other resources.

screens.title: Inference Objective and llm-d router
screens.lead: Select each tab to see how the InferenceObjective's priority alters the processing order in the queue, and where the implementation resides in the storage.

visual.alt: Diagram comparing the processing order of two requests with different priorities within the same queue.
labels: Applies only when resources are insufficient and a wait condition occurs

tabs.label: The meaning of priority
tabs.body: InferenceObjective is a resource that declares requirements for a specific model usage scenario and is managed by the inference workload owner. The core field priority is an integer, where higher values indicate greater importance. Negative values are allowed, and if not specified, it defaults to 0. For example, a request with priority 10 is always processed before a request with priority 0, and a request with priority -10 is always processed after a request with priority 0.

tabs.label: Chat request (priority 10)
tabs.body: Assign a high value to online chat requests that are sensitive to delay. When resources are insufficient and a request waits in a queue, this request is processed before other requests with lower priority within the same pool. Since the user is waiting on the screen, it is appropriate to prioritize this request.

tabs.label: Summary batch (priority -10)
tabs.body: For summary-style batch jobs that can tolerate delays, a low value is assigned. When the system is busy, this request waits behind. Fairness applies only among requests with the same priority, so lower-priority requests may be starved while higher-priority requests continuously arrive.

tabs.label: Target pool specification
tabs.body: InferenceObjective specifies which pool it applies to either by directly listing the pool name in `poolRefs` or by selecting a label using `poolSelector`. One of these must be present, and a label selection cannot be empty. The objective of pointing to all pools within a namespace at once is not supported.

tabs.label: llm-d router
tabs.body: The EPP, InferenceObjective API, InferenceModelRewrite API, and Body Based Router have been moved to the llm-d router repository. The original Gateway API Inference Extension repository continues to manage the InferencePool API, lightweight EPP (LWEPP), and compatibility verification. This project is accelerating LLM serving optimization in llm-d through collaboration with vLLM.

screens.outro: Now that all components have been delivered, let's apply them to the example.

screens.title: Explanation: The reason routing is needed to reflect request length and queue status
screens.lead: The instructor explains the case step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

visual.alt: A bar chart comparing the pending request count in the pod and the KV cache utilization.

steps.title: Situation: A short question followed by a lengthy summary is provided.
steps.body: A dozen short queries and one lengthy document summary arrive simultaneously. While the number of requests may seem trivial at first glance, the single long summary consumes considerable GPU and KV cache resources due to its length. The fact that costs vary per request is the key insight in this case.

steps.title: General distribution: divide sequentially
steps.body: If processed sequentially, the queue of pods receiving long summaries grows longer, causing even shorter requests to be delayed behind it. Since the load balancer sees all requests as identical, the response time for short requests—i.e., tail latency—degrades.

steps.title: Signal verification: status varies by pod
steps.body: EPP checks the metrics and finds that Pod B has nearly full KV cache. When it receives a new request, eviction from the cache will occur, causing slower performance. On the other hand, Pod C has zero pending requests and has available cache space.

steps.title: EPP Selection: Send to a spare pod
steps.body: EPP notifies the gateway to send a new request to pod C, which has a short queue and available cache. If a preloaded pod with a prefix cache or LoRA adapter is already available, that signal is also considered in the selection process. The selection is based on state rather than order.

steps.title: Priority: Interactive first, batch later
steps.body: Even if resources are insufficient and requests queue up, the InferenceObjective's priority takes effect. Interactive requests are processed first with higher priority, while summary batching requests wait behind. Remember that priority only affects the processing order when a queue actually forms.

steps.title: Results and Conclusions
steps.body: Tail latency is decreasing, and GPUs that were previously idle are now sharing work. Since inference requests have variable costs, work must be distributed based on server status rather than simply on request count. This is why inference routing is necessary.

screens.outro: I will summarize only the key points from the case.

screens.title: General load balancing and inference routing
screens.lead: This lesson summarizes the components and differences into one cohesive overview. Read it carefully and connect it with the examples previously discussed.

paragraphs: Inference Gateway is a configuration that combines EPP with the Gateway API proxy. While general load balancing selects servers based on paths or order, inference routing selects servers based on server state metrics such as KV cache utilization, queue length, LoRA adapters, and prefix cache.

InferencePool is a unit that groups pods sharing the same accelerator, same base model, and same model server configuration, and it has been stabilized in version v1. InferenceObjective declares which request to prioritize within the pool. It is clearer to distinguish between determining where the pool should send requests and determining which request the objective should process first.
Finally, remember that the model server must adhere to the specification that outputs indicators readable by EPP. Without signals, even the best router will yield nothing visible.

Let's go back to the opening scene. Even when we scale the pods to four, requests still concentrated on a single node because the load distribution mechanism did not monitor the actual workload. If we add the step of reading server status to the gateway, the same number of servers will result in much more balanced queues and GPU utilization.

callout.label: organizing
callout.text: Inference traffic incurs different costs per request. Therefore, routing based on server status is required.

glossary.def: A configuration that combines Endpoint Picker with Gateway API-compliant proxies to provide optimized routing and load balancing for self-hosted generative models.
A component that intercepts requests via ext-proc and reads model server metrics to select the most appropriate replica.
This is v1 API resource defining a pod group that shares the same accelerator, base model, and model server. It is also commonly referred to as infpool.
This is a resource that declares serving goals such as priority for specific model use cases and connects to the pool.
This is the router implementation moved to the new repository, consisting of the EPP and InferenceObjective API.

misconceptions.myth: The inference gateway is equivalent to a general L7 load balancer.
misconceptions.fact: The conventional approach selects a server based on path or order. In contrast, the inference gateway selects a server based on EPP, reading not only path and order but also server state such as KV cache, queue, and LoRA adapters.

misconceptions.myth: InferencePool is another name for Service.
misconceptions.fact: They overlap slightly but are not the same. InferencePool is not a protective shell that blocks services; rather, it is an abstraction that manages groups of LLM model servers on a pod basis and connects them to EPP.

misconceptions.myth: Increasing priority always results in faster requests.
misconceptions.fact: Priority affects the processing order only when resources are insufficient and requests are waiting. When there is no waiting, there is no difference, and fairness applies only within the same priority level.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: Inference traffic incurs different costs per request, hence routing based on server status is required.
The Inference Gateway is a combination of the Gateway API proxy and EPP, and the InferencePool is a set of pods targeted for routing.
The priority of InferenceObjective determines the processing order when a queue builds up.
General load balancing is based on path and order, while inference-aware routing is based on cache, queue, and adapter signals.

checks.q: When the Endpoint Picker (EPP) selects a model server replica to send a request, what signal does it refer to, unlike a conventional load balancer?
options: Whether the path of the requested URL and the header values conform to certain rules
KV Cache utilization, number of pending requests, active LoRA adapters among server statuses
The order in which pods are created in the cluster and the order of pod names
Hashed client IP value and connection establishment time
checks.explain: EPP reads indicators provided by the model server (KV cache utilization, number of pending requests, LoRA adapters, prefix cache status) and selects the optimal replica.

wrong.0: Path-header based routing is a general routing approach that does not reflect the internal server state.
wrong.2: Creation order or name order is independent of the workload and thus fails to alleviate bias.
wrong.3: IP hash does not indicate request cost or server status.
